question: What are the criteria for the providers and facilitators of Professional Learning and Development for structured literacy approaches?
reply:
I am advised by the Ministry of Education that the criteria for providers and facilitators focuses on four main categories: Research and Evidence, Professional Learning and Development (PLD), Measuring Impact and Facilitation. 

Providers are expected to show their expertise in:
• evidence informed practice based on current research on what has been shown to be effective, including the science of learning
• the elements of structured literacy approaches
• their principals of explicit and intentional teaching
• effective methods of building teaching capability and changing teaching practice
• determining the impact of facilitation on teaching capability, and student progress and achievement
• recognising and responding to reading and writing difficulties.

question: What percentage of cell intercom emergency calls at Mt Eden went unanswered in the 12 months to July 2025?
reply:
I am advised that Mt Eden Corrections Facility utilises the AUSTCO/Cell Guard intercom system, which includes a diversion feature designed to ensure timely response to intercom calls. Between the hours of 6:00am and 6:00pm, all intercom calls fall within the responsibilities of custodial housing unit staff, who are on shift within the units day to day. Any intercom calls that are not answered within 90 seconds during this shift are automatically diverted to the site’s Master Control team. While the system does not capture a specific data field to quantify the number of intercom calls subject to diversion, the diversion mechanism itself ensures that calls are not left unattended.

I am further advised that intercom calls made outside of the 6.00am to 6.00pm time are managed directly by the site’s Master Control team.

question: What role can nurse practitioners play in improving access to primary care for rural New Zealanders, if any?
reply:
I am advised that nurse practitioners are a highly valued asset in ensuring access and provision of safe, high‐quality care, especially for rural New Zealanders who find it hard to access general practitioners.

I am further advised that nurse practitioners have advanced skills and practice beyond the level of registered nurses. They most commonly work as part of an interdisciplinary team improving access to healthcare and have the ability to work autonomously to provide a full range of assessments, diagnostic tests, prescribing, and treatment interventions. 

I am also advised that the number of nurse practitioners working in primary care is growing. They are an important element for evolving and diversifying primary care teams and are able to support the development and scope of other primary care nurses.

question: What progress, if any, has been made in the quarter October to December 2024 in the priority area ‘Ensure surveillance information planning and outputs are developed and shared with communities and health professionals’ under ‘STRATEGIC DIRECTION 1: Surveillance, information and public health knowledge systems to drive action’ as part of the Aotearoa New Zealand Sexually Transmitted and Blood Borne Infection Strategy 2023-2030?
reply: I refer the Member to Written Parliamentary Question 15495 (2025).
referred_reply:
Published in March 2023, the Sexually Transmitted and Blood Borne Infections (STBBI) Strategy sets out a roadmap to 2030 to achieve an Aotearoa New Zealand where STBBI are prevented and where all people living with STBBI live long and healthy lives free from stigma and discrimination.
 
 Officials from across the Ministry of Health (the Ministry) and Health NZ have developed a cross-agency STBBI work programme to implement the STBBI Strategy with an initial focus on the HIV, hepatitis C and syphilis action plans that sit under it, as well as hepatitis B and contracts with other STBBI related non-governmental and community organisations such as the Needle Exchange Programme (NEP).

 The goals and objectives in the strategy are intentionally high-level and the Ministry expects activities being taken to deliver on the priority action plans noted above to contribute to these over time.
 
 Specifically in the quarter October to December 2024, the following activities were progressed, all of which contribute towards implementing the strategic approaches for the STBBI Strategy.
 
 • There continued to be a strong focus on connecting with refugee migrants and asylum seeker groups, Hauora Māori partners, needle exchange services and sex workers to support these communities to be able to deliver future HIV and sexually transmitted infection (STI) testing.
 • Procurement documents were completed to expand innovative HIV and STI testing services to priority populations. A request for proposal will commence in quarter three 2024/25.
 • A working group, primarily involving people living with HIV representing the priority population groups, completed community engagement to test key concepts and gather insights on HIV stigma. This will inform development of an HIV campaign to challenge stigma and discrimination.
 • In response to the increase in HIV cases in Fiji, officials presented to the heads of Public Service Agencies in Fiji to provide insight on the management of HIV in New Zealand. Health NZ is also working with stakeholders to raise awareness of HIV amongst the Pacific population in New Zealand and increase HIV and STI testing.
 • Training, endorsed by the Nursing Council and the Pharmacy Council, continued to be promoted for nurses and pharmacists to provide hepatitis C treatment without prescription. 
• The HIV Monitoring Plan was published in June 2024 to support and measure progress towards achieving the goals and targets of the HIV Action Plan. Work is underway to develop the first HIV Monitoring Report. This report is expected to be delivered mid-2025.
 • Work to develop a teaching package for midwives on syphilis and other STIs has progressed with consultation with subject matter experts. The New Zealand College of Midwives is working in collaboration with Ngā Maia Māori Midwives Aotearoa and Pacific Midwives Aotearoa/Moana Connect to deliver the training.
 • Work commenced on preparations for procurement to identify a provider to develop a national campaign to raise awareness of syphilis and promote testing in sexually active heterosexual people. The campaign aims to address the increasing rates of syphilis in New Zealand and the associated cases of babies being born with congenital syphilis.

question: Further to 46852 (2025), how many, if any, secure care admissions were extended at Oranga Tamariki's Te Puna Wai o Tuhinapo youth justice facility between 1 July and 31 December 2024, and, if any, were all in full compliance with the law?

question: What evidence, if any, has he seen that boot camps for young offenders are effective at reducing rates of youth offending?
reply: I refer the Member to my answer to WPQ 179 (2024).
referred_reply:
Information on the evidence regarding the effectiveness of military academies was provided in briefing B-0029.

In summary, international and domestic evidence has shown that ‘boot camps’, in and of themselves, are one of the least effective interventions when it comes to reducing offending and antisocial behaviour among young people. The research shows that “boot camps for juvenile offenders that included counselling, and boot camps with a primary focus on rehabilitation, were significantly more effective than other types of boot camp…"

The briefing also notes that the Military-style Activity Camp (MAC) programme was delivered from 2010 to 2016. The programme aimed to target the most serious and persistent young offenders and was delivered as a partnership between Child, Youth and Family (CYF) and the New Zealand Defence Force (NZDF), based at Te Puna Wai o Tūhinapō Youth Justice Residence in Christchurch. It was found that the residential component of the MAC improved the attitude and motivation of young people to address their offending. Using teamwork and a mix of structured and routine activities, the NZDF staff helped break down barriers and promote the principles of equity, respect for authority, and self-discipline in the young people. Eighty percent of MAC participants successfully graduated the residential programme.

question: Does the Minister agree with the Climate Change Commission's findings in the Monitoring Report on emissions reduction that the agriculture and transport sectors pose the largest risks to future emissions budgets?
reply:
I agree that when compared to the Commission's own demonstration path from 2022, its finding is sensible. That finding, however, was not based on the latest climate data and projections, nor informed by the policies this government is committed to progressing as a more cost-effective approach to reducing emissions. 

The Climate Change Response Act (CCRA) 2002 requires that an emissions reduction plans includes policies and strategies sufficient to meet the relevant emissions budget. The second emissions reduction plan will be published before the end of the year and will outline the Government's policies and strategies, including for the agricultural and transport sectors, to meet the second emissions budget. The plan is not required to also meet the third emissions budget. When released, the plan will detail how the Government will lay the foundation to achieve the third emissions budget.
